turns.q:
Your response was: "Looked at it. Checkout flow. Nearly missed the submit button. It barely registered visually — took a moment to find the action I needed."

We want to understand what you meant by "nearly missed the submit button", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The "Place Order" button is positioned at the very bottom of the layout, below a large "Continue Shopping" button, pushing the primary action to the lowest point on the screen with no surrounding space to distinguish it.

B) The "Place Order" button appears visually subordinate to "Continue Shopping" — it sits beneath a much larger, more prominent element, making it structurally secondary in the layout hierarchy.

C) There is no section label or heading grouping the "Place Order" button as the final checkout action — it sits detached from the Payment Details section with no structural indicator that it is the completion step.

D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to)

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.

Looking at those two buttons at the bottom of the layout — the large dark "Continue Shopping" block above and the lighter "Place Order" beneath it — what does that size and contrast difference tell you about which action this layout treats as the more important one?
turns.a: Two buttons. Bottom of the screen. One is dark and visible — 'Continue Shopping.' The other is barely there. Nearly the same color as the background.

turns.q: If someone arrived at this layout having just filled in their payment details, what would that low-contrast "Place Order" button lead them to conclude about whether they're actually ready to complete the purchase?
turns.a: Wasn't sure 'Place Order' was the step I needed. Looked like it might be a label, not a button. Sat with that before re-reading to check.

turns.q: Given that you had to re-read to confirm "Place Order" was actually a button — is that something someone would work through once and move on, or would that same ambiguity keep creating friction every time they reached this point in the layout?
turns.a: 'Continue Shopping' pulled the eye — looked like the action. 'Place Order' had nothing pulling toward it. Nearly treated the wrong one as the submit step. Re-read before moving.

turns.q: If "Place Order" were given the same visual weight as "Continue Shopping" in this layout — same size, same contrast — would the uncertainty you described disappear, or is there something about where these two buttons sit relative to the Payment Details section that would still leave it unclear which one completes the purchase?
turns.a: More visible. Bigger. Has to stand out — can't be the one you scan past.

turns.q: If the design team could only move or resize one element in this layout before it went to development, what specifically would you change — and where would "Place Order" need to sit relative to the Payment Details section for it to read as the completion step?
turns.a: Solid fill: brand color — dark blue, green, anything with sufficient contrast against white. White label text at 14–16px minimum. Standard primary button treatment. Distinction from 'Continue Shopping' needs to be legible: primary CTA gets the fill, secondary gets the outline or text link. Right now 'Place Order' is invisible and 'Continue Shopping' is visible. They're backwards. One CSS change to background-color, color, and font-size. Done.

missed_unlock_opportunities: After the participant said the 'Place Order' control looked like a label rather than a button and caused re-reading, the interviewer could have immediately asked for the underlying rule that makes a final purchase action recognizable.

When the participant said 'Continue Shopping' pulled the eye and nearly caused them to treat the wrong element as the submit step, the interviewer missed a chance to crystallize the hierarchy principle: the primary CTA must dominate secondary actions.

After the participant stated the CTA 'has to stand out' and cannot be scanned past, the interviewer could have pushed directly to a concrete design prescription earlier, rather than continuing near the same consequence level.
deflection_patterns_uncountered: The interview lingered on observable consequences and hesitation rather than consistently forcing the participant to articulate the design requirement behind them.
Repeated prompts stayed close to the same CTA hierarchy issue without sharply converting participant language into a value or rule statement.
The participant offered actionable visual design details only late in the chain, suggesting earlier prompts did not sufficiently demand specificity.
judge_report.overall_assessment: The interview successfully reached a concrete design rule for primary versus secondary checkout actions, but did so inefficiently with several repeated near-unlock turns. Stronger conversion from consequence to requirement earlier would have improved depth and reduced redundancy.
